papers.title: AgamOBP4-targeted drug repurposing identifies novel mosquito repellent scaffolds
papers.abstract: Odorant-binding proteins (OBPs) play central roles in insect chemoreception and represent attractive molecular targets for the discovery of novel behavior-modifying compounds. We report two crystal structures of Anopheles gambiae OBP4: one complexed with the fluorescent probe N-phenyl-1-naphthylamine and a second containing two indole molecules simultaneously bound within the ligand-binding cavity. Structural comparison revealed two binding subsites accommodating the aromatic moieties of 1-NPN or two indole molecules, while identifying Thr58 and Thr70 as key residues in ligand recognition. A structure-based virtual screening campaign was performed against a volatility-filtered library from DrugBank, FooDB, BioNet, and natural-volatiles datasets. Twenty-three ligands were selected for fluorescence competitive binding assays, identifying four AgamOBP4 binders with micromolar affinities (Ki = 2.4-21.8 M). Among them were benzoyl peroxide, an active anti-acne ingredient, Avex-73 (blarcamesine), a clinical-stage drug candidate, and 2-phenylethyl benzoate, a food- and fragrance-associated ester. Additional candidates include O,p'-DDE, a metabolite of the insecticide DDT, and fluorene, a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon detected in foods as environmental or processing-derived contaminants. Seven selected compounds were subsequently evaluated against Aedes albopictus in in-vivo behavioral assays, with benzoyl peroxide displaying the highest repellency (RI = 81.8% at 0.2 mg cm-2). AI-based protein-ligand modeling provided insights into ligand recognition and suggested relationships among binding mode, binding affinity, and bioactivity. Collectively, these findings establish the structural basis of ligand recognition by AgamOBP4, highlight the potential of drug-repurposing and food-derived chemical space as sources of next-generation mosquito repellents, and open new opportunities for the development of OBP4-based biosensors for food-quality and environmental monitoring applications.

papers.title: Automated DNA-Encoded Library Synthesis on Magnetic Anion Exchange Resin
papers.abstract: DNA-encoded libraries (DELs) access vast chemical spaces for drug discovery, but split-and-pool DEL synthesis remains the sole and very manual portion of the DEL workflow. Here, we automate DEL construction using diethylaminoethyl-functionalized weak anion exchange (WAX) magnetic resin and a KingFisher Apex particle-handling instrument. DNA encoding occurs in solution, followed by selective immobilization of DNA conjugates under low-salt conditions that exclude > 95% of unused encoding oligonucleotides. On-DNA chemistry then proceeds using the WAX resin-adsorbed "WAX-ON" DNA substrate in neat organic solvent. The platform supports amide formation, reductive amination, copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition, and Fmoc removal. Automated bead transfer enables iterative reaction and washing cycles. We synthesized two-cycle 9,216-member DELs from 96 Fmoc-protected amino acids and 96 carboxylic acids. Control selections reproducibly enriched the carbonic anhydrase ligand sulfamoylbenzoic acid. Magnetic WAX-ON DEL synthesis is compatible with diverse chemistries and uses the same instrumentation to automate end-to-end DEL preparation and affinity screening.

papers.title: Improved 1H NMR and ATR-FTIR approaches for structural characterization of high-G-block and high-M-block alginic acids isolated from sugar kelp by a two-step gelation method
papers.abstract: Two low-molecular-weight alginic acid fractions, G-block-rich SKP-G1 and M-block-rich SKP-G2, were sequentially isolated from a hot-water extract of sugar kelp (Saccharina latissima) alcohol-insoluble residue by acetic acid-induced and subsequent freeze-thaw-induced gelation. High-field (700 MHz) 2D 1H-1H COSY and TOCSY spectroscopy enabled comprehensive cross-peak assignments for selected alginate diad and triad sequences, supporting interpretation of 1D 1H NMR spectra. Sequence frequencies were combined with previously established inequalities [1] to calculate constrained frequency ranges for homoblocks beyond the triad level. For selected homoblock lengths up to a degree of polymerization of 18, comparison of the experimentally derived frequency ranges with frequencies predicted by chain-growth statistical models ruled out the Bernoulli model for both fractions and the first-order Markov model for SKP-G1. Applying the recently developed logarithmic cosine transformation (LCT) algorithm [2] to first- and second-derivative ATR-FTIR spectra enhanced the visualization of subtle spectral features and produced distinct fingerprints for the two fractions. As a proof of concept, LCT-transformed derivative ATR-FTIR spectra yielded distinct score distributions for the fractions in principal component analysis, suggesting their potential for chemometric differentiation of alginates with different block structures. In conclusion, extending 1H NMR-based sequence analysis to calculate constrained frequency ranges for homoblock polyads beyond the triad level, together with LCT-transformed derivative ATR-FTIR fingerprinting, expands the analytical toolkit for alginate block structure characterization.

papers.title: Sample Preparation and Homology-Driven Search Shape the First Holobiont Proteome of the Marine Sponge Viles ophiraphidites (formerly Topsentia ophiraphidites)
papers.abstract: Marine sponges are holobionts of host cells, extracellular matrix and dense microbial communities, and most lack reference proteomes. Viles ophiraphidites (formerly Topsentia ophiraphidites), a Brazilian demosponge, is represented in UniProtKB by a single protein. The study had two phases. In phase 1, four sample preparation workflows were compared on two specimens in 42 nLC-MS/MS runs: urea/thiourea in-solution digestion, acetone precipitation, S-Trap and GeLC-MS/MS. Every run was analysed with FragPipe and with a homology-driven pipeline that adds three layers to a rescored Sage search: the proteome of the closest sequenced relative (Halichondria panicea), MS-BLAST style alignment of de novo sequence tags, and error-tolerant interpretation of tag flanks. In phase 2, the selected workflow, S-Trap, was applied to four specimens in 12 runs. Both strategies ranked the workflows identically ({rho} = 0.98). S-Trap gave the deepest and most specimen independent proteome, with about 2,100 protein groups per specimen and an 8% difference between specimens, against 21-39% for the other workflows. The homology-driven layers raised assigned non-contaminant spectra by 21.3% in phase 1 and 26.8% in phase 2. They contributed 1,969 protein groups found only by homology and agreed with the database search on 99.5-99.9% of shared spectra. The proteome comprises 4,294 protein groups: 42% sponge and 58% bacterial or archaeal, the latter dominated by Poribacteria. It includes Nitrospira nitrite oxidoreductase detected in every run. The four phase-2 specimens had a similar composition (Bacteria 51-64% and Porifera 35-48% of peptides, Poribacteria alone 27-33%), whereas the two specimens stored long-term in ethanol at 4{degrees}C, which also differed in collection site and storage history, yielded four to five times less evidence than the frozen ones, even though reduction and alkylation had not been effective in the two frozen specimens. S-Trap combined with homology-driven search is a robust strategy for proteomics of non-model holobionts.

papers.title: Mechanism-Based Discovery of New TRIDs Targeting Ribosome Pockets
papers.abstract: Approximately 10% of all human pathogenic mutations are nonsense mutations which give rise to premature termination codon (PTC) diseases, leading to an estimated 35 million people worldwide who harbor such mutations. To date, no approaches leading to medical treatments which increase PTC readthrough have received FDA approval. However, one well-tolerated translation readthrough inducing drug (TRID), ataluren, was conditionally approved for 11 years by the European Medicines Agency for treatment of nonsense mutation Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy. In recent work we have shown that ataluren increases readthrough indirectly, by exclusively inhibiting termination without directly affecting readthrough by suppressor aminoacyl-tRNAs (sup-aa-tRNAs). Based on the idea that this mode of action (MoA) might be the reason for the low toxicity of ataluren, we have discovered potential new TRIDs, which target pockets within the ribosome to which the termination factor eRF1 binds but sup-aa-tRNAs do not. These new TRIDs, dipeptide derivatives of eRF1 and some Sartans, mimic the MoA of ataluren. Three Sartans, which are angiotensin II receptor blockers and FDA-approved for treatment of hypertension, are significantly more potent than ataluren in our reconstituted in vitro readthrough assay. These compounds might be more effective than ataluren in treating some PTC diseases. We anticipate that further development of these lead compounds will lead to more general effectiveness, used both alone and in combination with other classes of readthrough inducers.

papers.title: TransPepMS: A Tool to Verify Peptides Absent from Reference Proteomes
papers.abstract: Cells generate peptides absent from reference proteomes, including products of reverse proteolysis and gene fusions. These are an increasingly pursued class of targets in autoimmune disease, cancer vaccines and T-cell therapies. The sequence is itself the discovery, yet a convincing spectral match does not establish it, because an ordinary genome-encoded peptide of the same mass can explain the spectrum equally well. Independent benchmarking has identified this ambiguity as a dominant source of error in reported non-canonical identifications. Here, we introduce TransPepMS, which adjudicates each proposed assignment and returns a verdict of retained, unresolved, or rejected. For example, on adjudicating 1,154 reported proteasome-spliced immunopeptides, only 53 survived same-mass competition, whereas 91 of 99 insulin-spike hybrids were retained and all 46 planted canonical peptides were rejected, showing that TransPepMS discriminates genuine non-canonical peptides rather than merely deflating claims. TransPepMS provides peptide validation before they guide biological interpretation and immune-target selection.

papers.title: Molecular mechanism of albicidin-dependent transcription activation by the antibiotic resistance factor AlbA
papers.abstract: The escalating spread of antimicrobial resistance demands antibiotics with novel mechanisms of action. Albicidin is a potent DNA gyrase inhibitor produced by Xanthomonas species, and bacteria counter its activity through resistance mechanisms including the albicidin-sequestering protein AlbA from Klebsiella oxytoca. AlbA is a MerR family transcription activator that binds albicidin and stimulates expression of the albA gene, but how ligand recognition is coupled to transcription activation has remained unclear. Here, we use cryogenic electron microscopy and complementary biochemical assays to define the mechanism of AlbA-dependent transcription activation. Structures of transcription complexes reveal that AlbA remodels the promoter, repositioning the -35 element for productive sigma70 recognition and RNA polymerase engagement. Albicidin does not measurably alter AlbAs DNA affinity or the architecture of the mature open complex. Instead, transcription kinetics and experiments bypassing promoter opening indicate that albicidin selectively facilitates a promoter opening-dependent transition. AlbA is released upon synthesis of approximately five nucleotides, concomitant with downstream DNA melting, bubble translocation and upstream DNA rewinding rather than DNA scrunching. Together, these findings establish a sequential mechanism in which AlbA remodels promoter architecture, while albicidin tunes the kinetic transition to promoter opening, linking antibiotic recognition to induction of its sequestration machinery.

papers.title: Transglutaminase 3 is a Histone Monoaminylation Writer
papers.abstract: Histone monoaminylation, including serotonylation, dopaminylation, and histaminylation, is an emerging class of epigenetic modifications that regulates gene transcription in diverse physiological and disease contexts. Histone H3 glutamine 5 (H3Q5) was the first identified and remains a major site of monoaminylation on core histones. Mechanistically, monoaminylation involves the formation of an isopeptide bond between a substrate glutamine and a monoamine metabolite through a reversible transamidation reaction catalyzed by transglutaminases (TGs). Among the nine members of the human TG family, TG2 has been established as the major writer of H3Q5 monoaminylation. Here, we identify TG3 as an additional histone monoaminylation writer capable of catalyzing H3Q5 histaminylation (H3Q5his).

papers.title: Making the Impossible Possible: Uniting TMT and DIA for Scalable Low-Input-Proteomics
papers.abstract: Isobaric multiplexing using tandem mass tags (TMT) and data-independent acquisition (DIA) are two powerful techniques in quantitative proteomics, each offering distinct advantages. Combining these strategies provides synergistic benefits for low-input applications such as single-cell proteomics (SCP). However, integrating these strategies has remained challenging due to co-isolation interference and increased data complexity. Here, we present a systematic, identification-linked evaluation of a hybrid DIA-TMTpro 18-plex workflow on the Orbitrap Astral mass spectrometer (MS). Using a two-proteome interference model of human and yeast digests, we benchmarked quantitative accuracy and precision of TMT based DDA and DIA acquisition strategies across a range of isolation windows, injection times and input amounts. We provide READ (Reporter Ion Extractor and Annotation Director), an in-house developed Python-based tool which enables streamlined reporter ion (RI) quantification and co-isolation purity assessment. Using READ, TMT-based quantification becomes possible from DIA-focused search engines like Spectronaut or DIA-NN, which do not natively support TMT. We show that co-isolation interference drives both ratio compression and ratio inflation in TMT RI-based quantification regardless of acquisition mode. As an interference-resistant alternative, we further evaluated quantification via TMT complementary ions, which achieved near-label free quantitative accuracy at the cost of reduced plexing capacity and proteome depth. Together, these results establish practical guidelines for combining DIA and TMTpro on the Orbitrap Astral mass spectrometer and provide a foundation for extending DIA-TMT workflows to low-input applications such as SCP, where sensitivity, accuracy and throughput are critical.

papers.title: FBRSL1 couples ncPRC1.3 to CoREST to repress cell-cycle genes during human neuronal differentiation
papers.abstract: Most Polycomb complexes foster canonical gene repression, while noncanonical PRC1.3 (ncPRC1.3) unexpectedly activates transcription through its AUTS2 component. If and how ncPRC1.3 may also foster gene repression during development is unknown. Here, we show that in contrast to the impact of AUTS2 on ncPRC1.3, its paralog, FBRSL1, couples ncPRC1.3 to the CoREST/CTBP/LSD1 corepressor complex to mediate transcriptional repression. AUTS2 and FBRSL1 compete for binding to the RAWUL domain of the ncPRC1.3 subunit, PCGF3, and their isolated Atrophin-1 domains confer opposite transcriptional outputs. Corepressor interaction maps to a central Atrophin-1-containing region of FBRSL1, with CoREST and CTBP2 required for reporter repression. Patient-derived FBRSL1 truncations abolish this repressive capacity; specifically, the p.Gln163* variant retains PCGF3 binding, but loses corepressor association. In human embryonic stem cells carrying a homozygous p.Gln163* knock-in, cortical differentiation displays persistent cell-cycle gene expression and deficient neuronal gene induction. At the progenitor stage, chromatin occupancy of CoREST, CTBP2, PCGF3, and RING1B is lost and accessibility increases at cell-cycle promoters that subsequently fail to be repressed. Thus, FBRSL1 redirects ncPRC1.3 function by equipping the complex with a corepressor-linked repressive arm that restrains proliferative programs at the progenitor-to-neuron transition.

papers.title: Cryo-EM structure of the sub-50 kD PDZ-RhoGEF catalytic core-RhoA complex reveals an allosteric mechanism for GEF switch
papers.abstract: PDZ-RhoGEF (PRG) drives cellular processes including migration through activation of the GTPase RhoA. The GEF switch (GS) is an accessory region N-terminal to the PRG catalytic core that significantly enhances its activity against RhoA, but its mechanism is unknown. We take an integrative structural biology approach, including cryogenic electron microscopy, to deduce the GS mechanism. Enzymatic assays define interactions between the GS and PRG catalytic core that are required for enhancement of activity. While SEC-SAXS data suggest that the GS does not alter the global structure of the catalytic core-RhoA complex, HDX-MS data reveal that the GS induces widespread stabilization, particularly in the RhoA switch regions. We determined a sub-4 angstrom resolution structure of 46 kD of the complex between the catalytic core and RhoA, revealing that Switch I is more flexible without the GS. Collectively, these data suggest both direct and allosteric factors in the mechanism of the GS.

papers.title: Hexosyl transfer via a covalent intermediate within a dual retaining and inverting enzyme
papers.abstract: Bifunctional glycosyltransferases underpin biosynthesis of essential glycans, including bacterial capsular antigens, and eukaryotic glycosaminoglycans. Typically, these enzymes transfer hexose sugars from activated nucleotide-phosphate donors, forming new glycosidic bonds with either retention or inversion of anomeric stereochemistry. Retaining hexosyl transfer typically proceeds via non-covalent SNi-type pathways, but recent studies of octulosyl Kdo-transferases have reignited debate over covalent mechanisms. Here we comprehensively dissected the activity of the archetypal bifunctional glycosyltransferase PmHS2, providing X-ray structures of ligand complexes alongside atomistic simulations to delineate full substrate-to-product reaction trajectories. Combined computational, biochemical and evolutionary evidence suggests that PmHS2 retaining GlcNAc-transfer likely proceeds via a previously undescribed covalent mechanism, involving considerable assistance from departing nucleotide-phosphate rotation. In mapping reaction pathways, we also report the first example of a glycosyl donor substrate coopted as an acceptor, which enables enzymatic self-priming for polymerization. These new covalent and self-priming functionalities highlight unexplored routes to modulate or inhibit polysaccharide biosynthesis.

papers.title: High-fidelity bispecific protease KRysin for deeper plasma proteomics and phosphoproteomics
papers.abstract: Bottom-up proteomics relies on efficient and reproducible proteolytic digestion. Yet trypsin, the most widely used protease, frequently misses cleavages, particularly near prolines, acidic and phosphorylated residues. Incomplete digestion inflates search space, dilutes peptide signal, and limits depth and reproducibility, especially in challenging matrices such as plasma and phosphoproteomics. Here we present KRysin, a recombinant bispecific protease that cleaves C-terminal to lysine and arginine with very high specificity and efficiency, generating tryptic peptides compatible with standard proteomics workflows. In HeLa digests, ~99% of KRysin-generated peptides ended in lysine or arginine, including at sites followed by proline, and only 0.2% of peptides contained an internal (missed-cleaved) arginine and 6% an internal lysine, compared with 9% and 25%, respectively, for trypsin. Using narrow-window DIA at 60 samples-per-day, KRysin quantified close to 50,000 class I phosphosites, >10,000 more than trypsin-based workflows, and identified up to 40% more plasma protein groups, uniquely revealing receptors, cytokines, and growth factors. KRysin therefore provides a direct alternative to trypsin wherever digestion completeness, speed and PTM coverage are limiting.

papers.title: Ubiquitin isopeptidase and esterase activities have distinct catalytic requirements
papers.abstract: Post-translational ubiquitin signaling is reversed by dedicated proteases termed deubiquitinases, many of which utilize a cysteine-based catalytic triad to cleave the isopeptide linkage. This activity represents canonical isopeptidase activity that has been mechanistically well characterized. By contrast, non-canonical ubiquitination, linked instead by an ester bond, is reversed by esterase activity through a relatively less well understood process. Several deubiquitinases, including examples from pathogenic bacteria and humans, have been shown to harbor dual isopeptidase and esterase activities. Here, we show that while both functions can take place within the same active site, they exhibit distinct catalytic requirements. In fact, the catalytic cysteine itself is not strictly required for ubiquitin esterase activity, as highlighted by substantial residual activities in both bacterial and human deubiquitinases following the typical Cys-to-Ala substitution. A Cys-to-Thr substitution, meanwhile, effectively eliminates both isopeptidase and esterase activity. Further illustrating distinct catalytic requirements, cryptic ubiquitin esterase activities were identified in OTUD6B and OTULINL, two reportedly inactive human (pseudo-) deubiquitinases. Overall, our work establishes new perspectives and approaches for studying the regulation of non-canonical ester-linked ubiquitination.

papers.title: Structural basis of self-loading by replicative helicases
papers.abstract: DNA replication is conserved in all forms of life on earth, from subcellular structures such as viruses to human cells. Here we study a group of virus parasites whose replication is initiated by helicases like those found in simian viruses and eukaryotic cells. The process by which these viral helicases initiate the replication of the DNA remains poorly understood. Here, we show how the helicase binds the parasite's origin of replication with its carboxy terminal domains (CTDs) adopting flexible and different conformations. The CTD's flexibility moves the DNA towards the inside of the helicase's ring and bends the DNA at three discrete positions curving it. Our cryo-EM snapshots show that the helicase deforms the DNA while self-loading onto it as the first stage of the initiation of DNA replication, suggesting that initial melting and self-loading are coupled processes in this type of virus parasites.

papers.title: Reliable and Efficient Agentic Protein Design with Toolset Harnessing
papers.abstract: Computational protein design workflows require the orchestration of multiple tools, data formats, and analysis steps that are often fragmented. Here, we introduce Chaperone, a lightweight and customizable framework that enables seamless integration of RFdiffusion3 (RFD3) with downstream sequence design, structure prediction, and evaluation tools, including ProteinMPNN, AlphaFold3 (AF3), and more than 50 other protein design tools. By combining a programmable agent-friendly interface with parallelized execution on high-performance computing systems, Chaperone as a harness enables rapid iteration and scalable exploration of complex protein design workflows. Across an evaluation of nine biomolecular design tasks, we find using Chaperone reduces total token usage relative to baseline agents by 86% and GPU costs by 64%, while increasing the overall computational design pass rate. We demonstrate Chaperones utility for large-scale design-space exploration through a two-week end-to-end small-molecule binder design campaign, yielding low nanomolar binders to cortisol zero shot. We further demonstrate its versatility across distinct design challenges, including the design of a symmetric 12-subunit self-assembly nanoparticle and a linker that mediates interactions between C2- and D3-symmetric protein complexes to form crystalline assemblies. Together, these results demonstrate how agent harnesses built around standardized tool interfaces can substantially improve the efficiency and success of complex, long-horizon agentic design workflows in biology. We make Chaperone freely available to the community on GitHub: https://github.com/RosettaCommons/chaperone.

papers.title: Hypoxia reduces induced LRIG1 protein despite sustained mRNA induction in colorectal cancer organoids
papers.abstract: LRIG1 is a negative regulator of receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling that promotes tumor suppression by driving degradation of EGFR and other RTKs. Inducing LRIG1 expression has therefore been proposed as a strategy to limit cancer cell survival under hypoxia. However, whether hypoxia itself affects LRIG1 expression remains unclear. Here, we investigated how hypoxia affects LRIG1 expression and protein abundance in human cancer datasets and colorectal cancer organoids. Analysis of The Cancer Genome Atlas data across gastrointestinal and other cancers revealed an inverse association between LRIG1 mRNA expression and a hypoxia gene signature that persisted after adjustment for global gene expression. We previously showed that BMPR inhibition induces LRIG1 and suppresses colorectal cancer organoid growth through LRIG1. Under hypoxia, this growth inhibition in colorectal cancer organoids was attenuated, and LRIG1 protein accumulation was reduced despite sustained mRNA induction. Pre-induced LRIG1 protein declined within 3 h of hypoxic exposure in organoids, and ectopically expressed LRIG1 similarly decreased in HEK293 cells. Pharmacological HIF1 inhibition did not prevent LRIG1 protein loss under hypoxia, whereas HIF1 stabilization did not reproduce it under normoxia, suggesting limited HIF1 involvement. Bafilomycin A1 restored LRIG1 protein levels, whereas chloroquine and the proteasome inhibitor MG132 did not, implicating a bafilomycin A1-sensitive lysosomal process. Notably, the hypoxia-induced decrease in LRIG1 was not accompanied by a decrease in total EGFR. These findings suggest that hypoxia limits LRIG1 protein induction, potentially constraining strategies that rely on LRIG1 induction in cancer treatment.

papers.title: Evolution-Guided Engineering of Non-conserved N-Glycosylation Sites Improves Heterologous Production of Sulfotransferases
papers.abstract: Escherichia coli features low cost, mature fermentation technology and high recombinant protein output, but the expression of glycosylation-dependent eukaryotic proteins therein is severely limited. Many glycosylated proteins are key tool enzymes for the biosynthesis of various pharmaceutical molecules, such as glycosaminoglycan-related synthases, but there is a lack of universal protein engineering methods to enable the adaptive evolution of these enzymes in E. coli. We established an evolution-guided optimization strategy that targets non-conserved N-glycosylation sites (EGO-NGly). The core of this strategy lies in the phylogeny-guided selective reversion of evolutionarily acquired N-glycosylation sequons to naturally occurring non-glycosylated residues from early-divergent orthologs, thereby improving heterologous production and residual activity stability for selected sulfotransferases in E. coli. Using heparin 3-O-sulfotransferase 1 (3OST-1) as a model enzyme apparatus in eukaryotic organisms, EGO-NGly extended the residual activity half-life by 4.5-fold. Structural analysis and molecular dynamics simulations indicate that greater surface rigidity and remodeling of intramolecular interaction networks contribute to the improved conformational stability of M7 in an aglycosylated host. EGO-NGly was further applied to a panel of 3OST and 6OST homologs, demonstrating its applicability to a subset of the tested enzymes. Furthermore, EGO-NGly can be orthogonally integrated with other complementary protein engineering strategies, as exemplified by its combination with the machine learning-aided Protein Repair One-Stop Service, generating variants with 8-fold and 17-fold extensions in residual activity half-life. Collectively, these results establish EGO-NGly as a practical and potentially cost-effective engineering strategy for improving the prokaryotic expression and functional performance of selected glycosylation-dependent eukaryotic sulfotransferases.

papers.title: Untargeted metabolomics reveals a selectively enriched surface metabolome underpinning constitutive chemical defence in the red alga Halymenia floresii (Clemente) C.Agardh, 1817 ((Rhodophyta, Halymeniales)
papers.abstract: Abstract: Marine macroalgae rely on chemically mediated surface defences to prevent microbial colonization and fouling, yet the composition of surface-associated metabolites and their ecological roles remain poorly understood. In this study, untargeted liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry (LC/MS) based metabolomics was used to characterize the surface-associated metabolome of the tropical red macroalga Halymenia floresii and identify metabolites potentially involved in chemical defence. Selective dipping extraction (DIP) was used to recover surface-associated metabolites and compared with whole-cell metabolome (WCM) extracts. Across both datasets, 22,455 LC/MS features were detected, including 10,505 features in the surface extracts and 11,495 additional features detected only in the WCM extracts. Statistical filtering identified 722 LC/MS features consistently enriched by at least four-fold in surface extracts relative to WCM extracts. These features yielded 928 putative metabolite annotations using xMSannotator, with biological interpretation supported by KEGG, LIPID MAPS, and MassBank. Pathway reconstruction using the Lilikoi R package identified 44 metabolite pathway associations, predominantly involving lipid-associated metabolism, including steroidogenesis, arachidonic acid metabolism, plasmalogen synthesis, fatty acid biosynthesis, sphingolipid metabolism and sterol biosynthesis. Manual curation further indicated enrichment of fatty acids, oxylipin-like metabolites, sphingolipids, phospholipid precursors and isoprenoid intermediates at the algal surface. Rather than indicating the presence of metabolites unique to the surface, the findings suggest that H. floresii selectively enriches lipid-associated metabolites at the thallus seawater interface. Spatial localization of relatively hydrophobic metabolites may provide an energetically efficient chemical defence strategy by retaining bioactive compounds at the site where microbial attachment and biofilm formation are initiated while minimizing their loss to the surrounding seawater. Overall, this study demonstrates that chemical defence in H. floresii is associated with the selective surface enrichment of lipid-associated metabolites rather than the occurrence of unique surface-specific compounds, providing new insights into the spatial organization of macroalgal chemical defences and the mechanisms underlying resistance to microbial colonization and fouling.

papers.title: An integrated Rheo-NMR platform for real-time, site-specific kinetic analysis of amyloid formation
papers.abstract: Amyloid fibrils are protein aggregates associated with neurodegenerative diseases. Their formation proceeds through protein- and condition-dependent microscopic pathways that can generate structurally and biologically distinct aggregates, yet these pathways are inferred from ensemble-averaged measurements. Amyloid formation is often slow under quiescent conditions, prompting agitation. However, conventional agitation precludes simultaneous high-resolution solution nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, limiting site-specific kinetic analysis of microscopic aggregation pathways. Here we present an integrated Rheo-NMR platform combining controlled shear flow, time-resolved NMR spectroscopy and mechanistic kinetic modeling to quantify site-specific amyloid-formation kinetics in a single, continuously monitored reaction. Applied to -synuclein under dilute and polyethylene glycol (PEG)-induced liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) conditions, the method revealed environment-dependent redistribution of kinetic signatures associated with primary nucleation-elongation and secondary nucleation-elongation pathways across the sequence. The platform distinguishes changes in overall aggregation rates from differences in residue-specific kinetic profiles, providing a quantitative framework for dissecting environment-dependent amyloid formation.

papers.title: IRE1α undergoes a dynamic filament assembly cycle governed by unfolded proteins and BiP.
papers.abstract: The endoplasmic reticulum is a major hub of protein synthesis, modification and trafficking that relies on the Unfolded Protein Response (UPR) to balance its folding capacity. IRE1, the most conserved of the UPR sensors, undergoes a change in oligomeric state upon activation that propagates the stress signal from the ER lumen to its cytoplasmic kinase/RNase domains. Here we show that opposing inputs from unfolded proteins and the ER chaperone machinery govern a dynamic cycle of IRE1 assembly. A bona fide unfolded ER client directly binds the IRE1 lumenal domain (LD) and promotes higher-order oligomerization. Model peptides further reveal that full assembly into LD filaments depends on ligand length, sequence, and the IRE1 oligomerization interfaces. The ER Hsp70, BiP, counterbalances this process through two distinct mechanisms: i) an ATP-independent interaction via the BiP nucleotide-binding domain buffers early IRE1 assembly by engaging its oligomerization interface, whereas ii) ATP-regulated BiP/ERDJ machinery actively dismantles assembled filaments. Together, our findings reconcile direct unfolded protein recognition with BiP-mediated regulation to establish LD oligomerization as a point of integration through which unfolded protein load and chaperone availability dynamically regulate IRE1 assembly state and signalling.

papers.title: Hyperactivation of β-catenin rewires mitochondrial fuel selection in liver cancer cells
papers.abstract: Metabolic state is tightly linked to cell fate, and expression of the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC), which imports pyruvate into mitochondria, is a robust marker of it. The transcriptional regulators that set metabolic state, however, remain poorly defined. In the liver, {beta}-catenin is one of the determinants of metabolic zonation, and activating CTNNB1 mutations are frequent in hepatocellular carcinoma. Here we show that {beta}-catenin regulates metabolic state in liver cancer cells. An unbiased CRISPR screen that uses endogenous MPC1 transcript abundance as the marker identifies CTNNB1. Activating {beta}-catenin pharmacologically or genetically reduces MPC1 and MPC2 transcript and protein levels, and MPC expression is also low in {beta}-catenin-driven liver tumors in vivo. Beyond the MPC, {beta}-catenin activation impairs assembly of respiratory Complexes III and IV, reduces mitochondrial DNA content and respiratory capacity, elongates mitochondrial networks and remodels the lipidome. Stable isotope tracing shows reduced entry of glucose- and lactate-derived carbon into the TCA cycle alongside increased oxidation of palmitate and oleate. These findings identify {beta}-catenin as a regulator of metabolic state that drives a fuel switch from carbohydrate to fatty acid oxidation in liver cancer cells.

papers.title: HaloPROTAC-mediated degradation reveals SOX10-dependent gene expression changes in melanoma cells
papers.abstract: The transcription factor SOX10 is required for melanoma cell proliferation. However, SOX10 expression in single cells is heterogeneous, and low SOX10-expressing cells exhibit a dormant-invasive phenotype associated with drug resistance and metastasis. Despite longstanding interest in SOX10 as a diagnostic marker and potential therapeutic target in melanoma, the molecular mechanism and targets of SOX10 remain incompletely understood. New tools for the study and perturbation of SOX10 in cancer-relevant systems are needed to address these gaps in our knowledge. In this study, we engineered a patient-derived WW165 melanoma cell line for programmable SOX10 targeted proteolysis. We achieved this by replacing the endogenous copies of SOX10 with a SOX10-HaloTag transgene that supports cell growth, but can be rapidly degraded by the ubiquitin-proteasome system upon with a commercially available HaloPROTAC3 degrader molecule. We demonstrate that inducible degradation of SOX10-HaloTag faithfully recapitulates the known SOX10 transcriptional program, while also enabling discovery of SOX10 target genes previously undetected with standard genetic silencing approaches. We validated NAV2 and NCKAP5 as novel genes that are directly bound by SOX10 and coregulated with SOX10 expression in a patient cohort. This study demonstrates that new biological insights into the function of SOX10 can be enabled by targeted degradation and suggests that analogous approaches could prove powerful in the study of other transcription factors. We further suggest that the SOX10-HaloTag expressing melanoma cell line developed in this study could find further applications in investigating the consequences of SOX10 targeted degradation in vitro and in vivo.

papers.title: Heimdall SNAREs reveal an ancestral architecture of eukaryotic SNARE complexes
papers.abstract: SNARE proteins are central to eukaryotic cell biology, where they drive membrane fusion by assembling into four-helix bundles that bring opposing membranes into close proximity. Their ubiquitous role in intracellular membrane trafficking raises fundamental questions about their evolutionary origin and the emergence of eukaryotic cellular complexity. Here, we characterize SNARE-like proteins from Heimdallarchaeota, a lineage within the Asgard archaea that is closely related to eukaryotes. We show that a Heimdall SNARE forms a stable homotetrameric four-helix bundle in solution and determine its structure by X-ray crystallography. Strikingly, the Heimdall complex closely resembles eukaryotic SNARE complexes in its overall architecture and core organization, despite being composed of four identical subunits. Molecular dynamics simulations further reveal conserved physical features of the bundle alongside distinctive properties of its central 0-layer. These findings demonstrate that the characteristic four-helix architecture of SNAREs predates the emergence of eukaryotic cells and provide structural insight into the evolution of the membrane fusion machinery.

papers.title: Dual-portal ligand transport in human cytochrome P450 17A1
papers.abstract: Human cytochrome P450 17A1 (CYP17A1) is the qualitative regulator of steroidogenesis, catalyzing both 17-hydroxylation and 17,20-lyase cleavage at a single active site, and is the target of the prostate cancer drug abiraterone. Crystal structures show an almost fully enclosed site and do not reveal how lipophilic steroids reach it from the endoplasmic reticulum membrane or how the more polar products leave. We therefore asked which routes connect the CYP17A1 active site to the protein surface, and which of them are required. Molecular dynamics of the CYP17A1 enzyme followed by CAVER tunnel clustering produced 99 transport pathways in 14 clusters, which grouped by the elements forming their mouths into four topologically distinct portals (P-I to P-IV). Five structure-guided variants of CYP17A1 were expressed in HEK293 cells and both hydroxylase and lyase reactions were measured. Occluding the dominant P-I/P-II bottleneck (A105L) left both reactions intact and slightly raised them (116.1 {+/-} 8.0% hydroxylase, P = 0.0043; 134.8 {+/-} 27.9% lyase, P = 0.028). A tryptophan in the F/G lumen (L242W) was tolerated (96.6{+/-} 6.9% and 89.9{+/-} 10.4%, neither significant), whereas an engineered I205C/R239C pair across the same route abolished catalysis (below 2%, P < 0.001). Both perturbations of the membrane-facing P-IV portal cut activity below 2% of wild type (P < 0.001), and CYP17A1 protein levels accounted for neither phenotype. These data support a dual-portal model of vectorial ligand transport in CYP17A1.

papers.title: Olfactory neuroepithelium biomarker platform: a proof from Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: Unlike other diseases where target organs for biopsy are accessible, surrogate platforms are warranted for biomarkers of neuropsychiatric disorders due to the inaccessibility of the brain. We demonstrate a non-invasive platform combining a nasal soft-brush swab with single-cell Western blotting for neuron-specific protein analysis. Applied to Alzheimer's disease targeting phosphorylated tau, this demonstrated superior diagnostic capacity compared with blood-based approaches, indicating that the olfactory neuroepithelium is a sensitive biomarker platform.

papers.title: Development of a high throughput continuous fluorescence anisotropy-based assay to analyse peptidoglycan-digesting enzymes
papers.abstract: Bacterial cell wall processing enzymes have a central role in the control of the construction, remodelling and breakdown of the peptidoglycan wall that protects bacteria from osmotic rupture. Many of these enzymes have biologically essential functions and exert mechanistically diverse activities on a complex polymer substrate. Despite this biological importance they are relatively understudied and there are significant technical challenges in measuring the activity of individual enzymes against the complex chemical structure of the bacterial cell wall peptidoglycan. To generate a suitable substrate, bacterial cells are grown with a fluorescent D-alanine analogue, allowing the isolation of natively fluorescently labelled PG. This material is then used to measure interactions with PG-targeting enzymes and regulatory proteins. The resulting assay enables analysis of multiple enzyme-substrate combinations within minutes while retaining molecular specificity. This approach provides a robust, cost-effective alternative to conventional PG activity assays and could accelerate the identification and characterisation of novel antimicrobial compounds targeting bacterial cell wall metabolism. Our results indicate this assay has the potential to be employed in high-throughput inhibitor discovery, making it effective for a broad-spectrum assay for bacterial peptidoglycan research applications.

papers.title: Structural analysis reveals three families of bacterial tRNA mimics
papers.abstract: Comparative genomics has identified over 1,000 candidate structured RNA motifs, yet most remain functionally uncharacterized. Here, we combine crystallography, comparative analysis, and bacterial genetics to identify three families of bacterial tRNA-like RNAs. The skipping-rope RNA adopts an L-shaped fold resembling tRNA despite distinct secondary-structure connectivity and tertiary interactions. In Clostridioides difficile, the skipping-rope RNA RCd1 is abundantly expressed and processed into a highly stable RNA species. RCd1 overexpression suppresses sporulation, whereas its deletion enhances early spore formation, supporting a role in sporulation control. Guided by the skipping-rope structure, we identify a conserved architectural core and use it to recognize additional candidate tRNA mimics. Crystal structures of DUF2693-FD and salivarius-1 RNAs confirm a shared tRNA-like scaffold assembled through distinct interaction networks. Together, these findings expand the repertoire of bacterial tRNA mimics and establish a structural framework for recognizing shared architectures among uncharacterized ncRNAs, linking one such family to bacterial developmental regulation.

papers.title: Chemical proteomics suggests sofosbuvir is metabolically attached to proteins through a UMPylation-like pathway.
papers.abstract: Sofosbuvir is a pronucleotide prodrug (ProTide) that releases a uridine monophosphate analogue, which could modify proteins chemically or through UMP-transferring enzymes. Using an alkyne-tagged probe and chemical proteomics, we identified about 120 labelled proteins and a UMPylation-like (+774.31 Da) modification on cathepsin Z, suggesting that nucleotide prodrugs may enter protein nucleotidylation pathways.

papers.title: Enhanced Fidelity and Sequence Generality of an RNA Polymerase Ribozyme
papers.abstract: Directed evolution has been used to develop RNA enzymes (ribozymes) that catalyze the RNA-templated polymerization of RNA. The more advanced polymerases can synthesize long RNA products, but have shortcomings with regard to copying accuracy and template sequence generality, which are impediments to using the polymerase to replicate and evolve other functional RNAs. By applying stringent selection pressure over the course of 33 successive rounds of evolution, both the fidelity and sequence generality of the polymerase were greatly improved. When synthesizing large functional RNAs such as the class I ligase ribozyme, the fidelity improved from 86% to 94% per nucleotide, due to both reduced incorporation of mismatched nucleotides and reduced propensity to extend partial-length products that have mismatched termini. The improved polymerase is also able to synthesize a broad range of RNA products, including those that require copying templates that are highly structured or contain sequences that previously were difficult to copy.
